stem: Which of these is the best thermal conductor?

options.content: Copper
Wood
Plastic
Air

explanation: Metals such as copper are good thermal conductors.

stem: A metal bench and a wooden bench have been in the same shade all day. Why does the metal one feel colder to touch?

options.content: Metal conducts energy away from your hand faster.
The metal is at a lower temperature than the wood.
options.rationale: Both are at the same temperature.

options.content: Wood produces a little heat of its own.
Metal reflects the body heat away from your hand.

explanation: Both are at the same temperature; the metal is a better conductor, so it takes energy from your hand faster.

stem: Why do cooking pots have metal bases but plastic or wooden handles?

options.content: Plastic is a better conductor than metal, so it cools the pan.
Metal conducts heat to the food; plastic and wood insulate the handle.
Metal handles would melt and bend at normal cooking temperatures.
Wooden handles conduct energy into the food from the hand.

explanation: The metal base conducts energy well into the food; insulating handles protect the cook's hand.

stem: In conduction, the material itself moves to carry the energy from the hot end to the cold end.
explanation: In conduction the material stays in place; energy is passed from particle to particle. Movement of the material carrying energy is convection.

stem: Why are metals much better thermal conductors than non-metals?

options.content: Metal atoms do not vibrate, so they waste no energy on the way.
Metals have a lower density, so energy moves through faster.
options.rationale: Not the reason; many are dense.

options.content: Non-metals have no particles to pass the energy along.
Metals have free electrons that carry energy quickly through them.

explanation: As well as lattice vibrations, metals have free (delocalised) electrons that move quickly and transfer energy in collisions.
hints: What do metals contain that non-metals do not?

stem: Why are gases very poor thermal conductors?

options.content: Gas particles do not move, so they cannot pass energy on.
Gas particles are too small to carry energy from one to the next.
options.rationale: Particle size is not the reason; the large spacing is.

options.content: Their particles are far apart, so energy-passing collisions are rare.
Gases contain free electrons that carry the energy away.

explanation: With particles far apart, energy is passed on only in occasional collisions.
hints: Think about the spacing of gas particles.

stem: A learner compares how well copper, aluminium and iron conduct. She fixes a rod of each metal into the side of a tank of hot water, with a drawing pin stuck to the far end of each rod with wax.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which pin is likely to fall first?

options.content: The one on the iron rod
options.rationale: Iron is the poorest of the three.

options.content: The one on the aluminium rod
options.rationale: Aluminium is good, but copper is better.

options.content: They all fall together
The one on the copper rod
options.rationale: Correct: copper is the best conductor of the three.

parts.explanation: Copper conducts best, so its wax melts first.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State two things she must keep the same for a fair test.

points.description: The rods have the same length and thickness (diameter)
The wax blobs/pins are the same size and the rods start at the same temperature, all in the same hot water

explanation: The best conductor melts its wax first; a fair test controls the rods' dimensions, the wax and the heat source.
hints: Which variables could affect how quickly the wax melts?

stem: Why do woollen jumpers and blankets keep people warm?

options.content: Wool produces a little heat of its own.
Wool is a good conductor of body heat.
They trap air, which is a poor conductor.
Wool reflects the cold back outwards.

explanation: Wool fibres trap still air, a very poor conductor, so energy escapes from the body slowly.

stem: What name is given to a material that conducts thermal energy badly?
explanation: A thermal insulator, such as wood, plastic, wool or trapped air.
